source.title: CycleAlign: Iterative Distillation from Black-box LLM to White-box Models for Better Human Alignment
source.authors: Jixiang Hong; Quan Tu; Chang-Yu Chen; Xing Gao; Ji Zhang; Rui Yan

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses black-box LLM feedback to train white-box models and reports the performance of its iterative alignment method. It does not test the weak-supervisor/strong-student condition or measure PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper reports AI-feedback distillation results, but does not establish that its black-box supervisor is weaker than its student; its own results compare alignment methods and evaluate human alignment rather than weak-to-strong generalization. The reported findings are recorded under fits_no_version. PPO and RRHF results identified as cited are not recorded as this paper's own results.
record.test_reason: CycleAlign distils alignment from ChatGPT, a stronger black-box teacher, into LLaMA-7B and Alpaca-7B students. This is strong-to-weak distillation, the opposite of the weak-supervisor/strong-student setting. No PGR or student-vs-weaker-supervisor comparison is reported. The paper (Oct 2023) predates and does not cite the original (Dec 2023), so it cannot use the finding as a tool. T6 fits better than the reader's T4. No relation value fits exactly: the paper neither cites nor discusses the claim, and cites_only is the closest.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that iterative black-box/white-box interaction with dynamic ICL demonstrations improves harmlessness and helpfulness alignment of white-box models over RRHF/PRO. They claim state-of-the-art results approaching ChatGPT.
record.recipe_differences: The study iteratively fine-tunes LLaMA-7B or Alpaca-7B using black-box ChatGPT rankings, self-rankings, and agreement-derived in-context demonstrations; it does not use or measure the weak-to-strong PGR setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports changes with dynamic demonstrations and ICL ablations and with maximum interaction number N; it describes reward as increasing then decreasing across tested N settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Students trained on ChatGPT rankings reach reward scores of 68.4–69.0 total, below ChatGPT's own zero-shot 70.43, and improve over RRHF/PRO baselines. Agreement-ranking demonstrations derived from the student raise ChatGPT's ranking accuracy (0.664 to 0.687).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Iterative AI-feedback ranking distillation with dynamic in-context demonstrations improves reward-model and judge-rated alignment of 7B models over ranking-based baselines, with outcomes varying by subset and evaluator.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study does not compare a student trained on labels from a weaker supervisor or report PGR. Evaluation uses a reward model that the authors say may have limitations, and the text does not report uncertainty estimates for the main scores.
record.rows_left_out: No substantive reported results were left out. PPO and RRHF results explicitly cited from other work were not included.

untested.parts: No weak supervisor; the supervisor (ChatGPT) is stronger than the 7B students, and no PGR is computed.
Methods are compared on reward scores, not on PGR over naive weak-label fine-tuning.
No variation of supervisor or student size, and no PGR predictors.
No tests of weak-supervisor blind spots, distribution shift, or shared errors.

record.verdict_notes: The supervisor-student direction is strong-to-weak (ChatGPT teaching 7B models), so nothing here bears on weak-to-strong generalization. The reader's T4/uses_without_test label is wrong because the paper predates and does not rely on the finding. Rows r26 and r27 are duplicates. The reward model disagrees with GPT-4 and human judges on Harmless-base: the reward model scores PRO higher, while the judges prefer CycleAlign.

versions.untested_parts: No weak supervisor is tested, and PGR or a comparison of the student against a weaker labeling supervisor is not measured.
The paper compares its CycleAlign method and ablations, but does not test whether training changes raise PGR over naive weak-label fine-tuning.
No PGR dependence on supervisor or student size, task, or representations is measured.
The paper does not test weak-supervisor blind spots, distribution shift, or shared-error effects.
No theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor are tested or developed.
No vision or other non-language modality is tested.

relation.reason: The text discusses related AI-feedback alignment and distillation but contains no citation to weak-to-strong generalization or its original study. Among the listed relations, discusses describes this background-only connection.

tranche.reason: CycleAlign transfers alignment from ChatGPT to LLaMA-7B and Alpaca-7B. It neither tests nor uses the claim that a stronger student trained on weaker supervision beats its supervisor.

source_check.notes: These are alignment-method comparisons and ablations, not evidence for any listed weak-to-strong version; none/cannot_determine is appropriate. The RRHF baselines are cited from Song et al. (2023), and r26 duplicates r16.
